rationale:
My lens: I open this site most days to answer three questions - what's flying next, can I watch it, did it slip - and once or twice a week I go play Space Tycoon. I judged the three briefs on how fast they answer those questions on a phone at night, and on whether they give me a reason to click the game.

Mission Control (B) wins because it is the only one where my entire daily visit is satisfied in the first 844px with zero scrolling: mission name, T-13h clock, payload/orbit/booster, 'SLIPPED 2x since Jun', Watch live, and 'Remind me at T-1h, no account needed' - then the next-five rail. It is also the only brief that treats the mission NAME as the headline rather than the vehicle or the clock. Its Phase 1 catches real bugs I live with: LandingHero.tsx:229-230 uses <br className="hidden sm:block">, so the site's own headline renders as 'Every launch.Live, tracked,explained.' on my phone today.

Terminal (A) is the better return-visit page and by far the better game pitch - a live leaderboard next to live commodity spot prices is the single most persuasive thing anyone proposed for Space Tycoon. But its own brief names the risk correctly: 13px mono monochrome, no photography anywhere, and the launch is a clock rather than an event. Launch day should not feel like a trading desk.

Editorial (C) has the best single idea of the three - the LiveRail, a server-rendered countdown line in the masthead of every page. But the front page it proposes is not for me: the lead is an 8-minute Artemis essay and the launches are a 360px sidebar, and a cream ground for a night-time launch check throws away the one aesthetic advantage a space site has.

One caveat I'll own: B's central bet is region art behind the hero, and the mockup renders that as an empty dark placeholder, so I could not see the thing the brief rests on. Also: there is no public game-market API today (src/lib/game/spot-price.ts is server-side only, nothing under src/app/api/game/), so the live Tycoon market panel A and C both promise is cheap but not free.

scores.strengths: The only brief where my whole daily visit fits in one phone screen with no scroll - rendered at 390x844: GO pip, vehicle+pad, mission name, date, T-13h clock, all four telemetry pairs, both CTAs, and the first two next-five cards. It leads with the mission NAME. 'Remind me at T-1h, no account needed. One email at T-24h, one at T-1h, one if it scrubs' is the best conversion ask in any of the three. 'SLIPPED 2x since Jun' as a front-page telemetry tile is proprietary data nobody else surfaces. The rule that one launch URL has three states (T-, LIVE, FLEW/SCRUB with a debrief) would have made the 8/26 'every flown launch was scrubbed' bug impossible to hide. Its Phase 1 catches the broken mobile headline. The eight-region art grid as a shared visual key makes the site and the game feel like one world.
scores.weaknesses: The fold is one launch. On a Tuesday when the next thing is six days out, 900px of ember countdown is a poster, not information. The next-five rail is a thin 168px-card strip where it should be the second-most-important block. Its whole aesthetic bet is region art behind the hero and the mockup renders that as an empty dark placeholder. The game gets a violet band with a Play button: a poster, not proof, and the weakest game treatment of the three. Killing IndustryTicker outright removes the element with the highest information-per-pixel on a phone.
scores.graft: The hero's honest-data pair: 'SLIPPED 2x since Jun' promoted to the front page, plus 'Remind me at T-1h - no account needed, one email at T-24h, one at T-1h, one if it scrubs.'

scores.strengths: The best return-visit page of the three. In the 1440 render, without scrolling past ~1700px: six upcoming launches with T- times and pads, three wire stories, two AI insights, five tickers, private-funding totals, cost-to-orbit for four vehicles, a launch-cadence chart, a five-row rockets table and the Tycoon leaderboard. The /rockets 'table wearing a costume' observation is correct. Best game treatment by a distance: a live leaderboard beside live commodity spot prices is proof the economy is running before I register. The colourblind rule (glyph + sign + label, never colour alone) is the most rigorously enforced of the three. Turning the persona modal into a one-line dismissible strip under the ticker is the right shape.
scores.weaknesses: It is cold, and its own risk section admits it. 13px base, JetBrains Mono everywhere, monochrome ink, zero photography on the homepage, APOD exiled. The launch is a clock rather than an event: 'RFA One' renders at roughly half the weight of the countdown digits. The 1440 render has ~150px of dead space under MANIFEST and WIRE where three unequal columns fail to bottom-align. Deleting AnimatedCounter, StarField, HeroArt and every gradient removes 2,400 lines that display no numbers - defensible, and also every trace of delight.
scores.graft: The Space Tycoon landing panel: live public leaderboard beside live commodity spot prices, both server-rendered. getPublicLeaderboard already exists; spot prices exist in src/lib/game/spot-price.ts but have no public route yet.

scores.strengths: The LiveRail is the best single idea in all three documents: one server-rendered line at the top of every page. It fixes a real embarrassment - LandingHero.tsx:79-88 initialises nextLaunch, weatherSummary and fundingValue to '-' and fetches in a useEffect, so 'Every launch. Live, tracked, explained.' ships as four em-dashes to every crawler and every first paint. The mockup is the most finished of the three - a real rendered chart with completed/failed series, source line, permalink, PNG and table. Promoting /chart to 'Chart of the Week' on the front page is the cheapest credibility win available. Best pitch for the game: it uses the real sentence from space-tycoon/about/page.tsx:83 plus a live market chart, the leaderboard, the eight-region grid and the dev log.
scores.weaknesses: The front page is not built for me. The lead is an 8-minute Artemis II essay at 720px and the launches are a 360px sidebar; at 390px I get the rail, then a full screen of serif essay plus a hero-art block before 'NEXT FIVE LAUNCHES' appears. The paper ground is actively wrong for a night-time launch check, and the Tailwind compatibility layer it needs (929 files hardcode text-white) is admitted debt. Fraunces as body copy sitewide is a strong opinion with no bearing on why I visit. 3,464px desktop / 5,256px mobile is the tallest of the three.
scores.graft: The LiveRail - a server-rendered, cached-60s, one-line next-launch countdown in the masthead of every page, failing to a static 'Next launch ->' link and never to '-'.

rationale:
My lens: would I quote this site in an IC memo, and would I forward the link to a colleague who bills by the hour? That reduces to four tests - is the number citable (source and as-of), is it dense enough that I don't scroll for facts, does it show me something nobody else has, and does the chrome signal 'instrument' or 'brochure'.

I verified the shared factual spine: company-profiles/page.tsx:1 and mission-control/page.tsx:1 are both 'use client'; LandingHero.tsx initialises three fields to '-' and fetches in a useEffect; Navigation.tsx:461 points 'Jobs' at /space-talent. All true.

The claim that decided a lot of the ranking: Brief B alleges the homepage fabricates a funding figure on API failure. It does - LandingHero.tsx:171-172 sets '$2.1B' / 'VC Funding (est.)' and :177-179 sets '$2.1B' / 'VC Funding Q1 (est.)' in the .catch(). Two different labels, one invented number, in the same tile format as the real ones. That is a disqualifying trust defect, and only one of three briefs found it.

Density, measured on the rendered mockups: Terminal 1,730px desktop, Mission Control 2,542px, Editorial 3,464px, against 11,045px live. Terminal is the only mockup that puts a real table on the front page, and its markets rail is the only object across the three I would screenshot into a deck as-is.

Where Terminal loses points and Editorial gains them is the chart. Terminal's 'launch cadence' is grey bars with no axis, scale or legend. Editorial's is a proper figure with axes, a Completed/Failed legend, and a source line naming the record count and as-of timestamp. That single frame is worth more to me than the rest of Editorial's front page.

On differentiation, Mission Control is alone in noticing that schedule slip is the site's proprietary asset and putting it on the homepage hero. As a BD person at a launch company, competitor schedule reliability is the number I cannot get cleanly anywhere else. Best idea in the set, weakest-scoring layout for my lens.

Editorial scores lowest not because it is bad but because a magazine is not a terminal, and the brief itself pre-authorises abandoning its paper ground. When a proposal names its own escape hatch, the escape hatch is the plan.

scores.strengths: Highest citability per pixel. The rockets table on the front page - vehicle, operator, $/launch, LEO tonnage, reliability, 90d cadence, next flight - is the one object across all three mockups I would paste into a deck without editing. Provenance is systematic: every panel header carries 'source, updated 14:32Z'. The error doctrine is the most professionally sound thing in the set: on fetch failure keep the last good value, dim it, badge it stale with a timestamp; reserve a full-panel error for data that has never existed. That rule would have prevented the $2.1B bug outright. The colourblind contract means tables survive a projector and a greyscale print. Measured 1,730px desktop against 11,045px live.
scores.weaknesses: The launch-cadence chart is grey bars with no axis, scale, legend or y-values - on a page whose argument is 'the data is the interface', the only chart is the least credible object on it. The 1440 layout has ~200px of dead space under The Wire. 13px base with 12px cells is aggressive against a stated enthusiast-first audience. Brand-wise it is a Bloomberg clone - nothing about it says 'space'. It underserves the narrative half of intelligence. And it missed the fabricated-fallback bug.
scores.graft: The stale-data doctrine plus panel-level provenance: every panel header carries 'label, source, updated HH:MMZ', and on fetch failure the panel keeps its last good value dimmed with a 'STALE, last good 13:58Z, retrying' badge rather than blanking or substituting.

scores.strengths: The only brief that found the site's actual credibility bug: LandingHero.tsx:171-172 and :177-179 hardcode $2.1B as two differently-labelled 'estimates' when the API fails. It also kills the '61% Avg Completeness' tile on /company-profiles - an internal data-quality metric displayed as industry intelligence. Best differentiation argument in the set: 'SLIPPED 2x since Jun' as a first-class hero telemetry field plus a slip-history panel captioned 'Nobody else records this'. Provenance is handled at the right altitude - one 'as of, source' line under the telemetry row. Phase 1 is four days of pure deletion, reversible in one revert. The strongest accessibility work: aria-live='off' on a per-second countdown, and the observation that AnimatedCounter/ScrollReveal drive animation through requestAnimationFrame, which the CSS reduced-motion clamp never reaches.
scores.weaknesses: The hero spends roughly 650px of a 900px desktop fold on one launch; I arrive from a search for a company, not a countdown. The industry half is four telemetry tiles and three news cards - the thinnest business content of the three. The mockup contains zero <table> elements despite specifying a DataTable component, so the density claim is asserted rather than demonstrated. Ember-on-black plus the violet Tycoon band reads consumer-gaming - the wrong signal when the link lands in an IC channel. The eight-region-art system is lovely, is Phase 3, and is correctly first to be cut.
scores.graft: Two cheap things: delete the fabricated fallbacks at LandingHero.tsx:171-179 and the '61% Avg Completeness' tile; then promote slip count to a headline telemetry field wherever a launch or a company appears, captioned as proprietary.

scores.strengths: The most credible-looking artefact of the three, and one element beats everything in the other two: the Chart of the Week is a properly drawn figure with axes, gridlines, a Completed/Failed legend, a labelled peak, and a source line naming the record count and as-of timestamp. It is the only chart across the three mockups I would paste into a memo. 'The Numbers' is the correct pattern for a stat strip - four figures, each linking to the page that owns it, under one shared source line. The rule that every company profile gets one authored sentence is the highest-value idea for my side of the audience. The LiveRail as a server-rendered line in the root layout is the cleanest fix for the '-' placeholder problem and is layout-independent. Honest measurement of the migration blast radius.
scores.weaknesses: It is a magazine, and I do not read magazines for procurement decisions. 3,464px of desktop front page whose entire industry content is four stat tiles. The paper ground is a real trust hazard in this vertical. The brief concedes the Tailwind compatibility layer is a hack and pre-authorises abandoning paper - what remains is warm ink plus better typography, which is not a redesign. Fraunces as body copy is an unforced bet on the guides that carry ~54k impressions a quarter. 22 days, with the risk loaded into Phase 2.
scores.graft: The ChartFrame done to publication standard - title, one-line deck, real axes and legend, and a footer naming the source, the record count, the as-of timestamp, and permalink/PNG/table. Plus the one-authored-sentence rule for every company profile.

rationale:
Lens: the engineer who has to build this with one founder and an AI. I judged on migration cost, reuse of what's already paid for, a11y, performance, coherence with the existing Tailwind system, and I penalized anything that needs a rewrite.

The measurement that decides it. I reproduced Brief C's audit: of 1,497 .tsx files, 929 hardcode text-white, 903 hardcode bg-white/[...], 765 hardcode text-slate-400, and only 58 read var(--text-*). --accent-primary is read by 13 files, while indigo-* appears in 114, cyan-* in 246, purple-* in 286, amber-* in 308. globals.css already carries a --v2-* alias block and a 'V3 REDESIGN' comment - this codebase has been redesigned twice and the tokens never propagated. So: re-valuing tokens changes almost nothing on this site. Any brief that budgets a palette change as a token edit is wrong by an order of magnitude, and any brief that changes the page ground is a 900-file rewrite.

That single fact ranks them. Brief A budgets 1.0 day for 'new token values under existing token names, so every consumer inherits' - flatly false here. Brief B doesn't measure it either, but B is the only one that designs a mechanism for the biggest real cost (a codemod-able alias layer for .card-*, which I measured at 352 files, not its stated ~120). Brief C measured it correctly, then proposed a paper ground anyway behind a Tailwind-utility override hack it calls 'debt with a named owner' - the failure mode this lens penalizes hardest.

Other things I checked: mission-control/page.tsx:1 and company-profiles/page.tsx:1 are both 'use client'; src/app/rockets/page.tsx is 82 lines of grid-cols-3 cards, server-rendered, so A's table conversion really is about an hour; 149 files hand-roll <table> and no DataTable primitive exists; MobileTableView and VirtualList have 2 call sites each (C's 'about 6 of ~40' is optimistic); ScrollReveal has 182 call sites, so A's 'deleted on sight' list quietly contains a 182-file edit it never priced, while B's answer - one useReducedMotion() hook wired into the component - is the cheap correct fix; the 24 public/game/region-*.webp already have a loader (RegionBackdrop.tsx, src/lib/game/assets.ts); src/lib/charts/{registry,render,data}.ts and /chart exist as C says; SearchCommandPalette.tsx already exists at 960 lines. None of the three re-proposes anything from ROADMAP_2026-09.md's rejected list.

Rendered heights (fullPage): terminal 1,730px desktop / 3,704 mobile; mission-control 2,542 / 3,975; editorial 3,464 / 5,256 - against 11,045 / 15,667 live today.

Winner: mission-control. Its Phase 1 is four days of deletion in two files, ships and is measurable on its own, reverts in one commit, and requires none of its own design system. It stays on a dark ground so the 929 text-white files keep working with no compatibility layer. Its a11y findings are the only ones that are real defects with file:line and cheap fixes. And its cut-list degrades gracefully: cut Phase 3, the fonts, and the palette, and you still have the four days that give the fold back.

scores.strengths: Phase 1 is 4 days of pure deletion from src/app/layout.tsx:297-304 and src/app/page.tsx - no new design system, ships alone, measurable alone, revertible in one commit. It is the only brief that designs a migration mechanism for the largest real cost: a codemod-able alias layer mapping .card-* -> .console so existing call sites keep rendering during migration (I measured 352 files matching the card classes). It stays on a dark ground, so the 929 text-white and 903 bg-white/ files need no compatibility layer. Its art layer reuses 24 region-*.webp that already have a loader. It keeps DM Sans and lists the font swap as cut #2. Its a11y findings are the only genuine defects in the set, each with a file:line and a cheap fix: rAF counters with no reduced-motion guard, text-[7px] at LandingHero.tsx:274, duplicate breadcrumbs in four named files, aria-live='off' on the countdown, and the <br className="hidden sm:block"> that renders 'Every launch.Live, tracked,explained.' at 390px. useReducedMotion() as one hook is the cheapest correct answer to ScrollReveal's 182 call sites. Best mobile fold of the three.
scores.weaknesses: The indigo->ember swap is one line in Phase 2 with no propagation plan, and the hues it replaces are hardcoded in Tailwind utilities across 114/246/286 files. Its own cut-list puts the palette at cut #4, which leaves Phase 2 without much identity. Full-bleed 21:9 region art above the fold is an LCP liability the brief never costs; the mockup shows the hero as near-black without it. Per-image scrim contrast QA across 8 paintings x ~30 surfaces is fiddly manual work with no automated test. It claims the region art is 'referenced exactly once' - actually there is a RegionBackdrop component and an assets.ts map. 16 days, and it says itself Phase 3 is the least load-bearing.
scores.graft: Phase 1 verbatim, whichever design wins: strip TrialBanner, AnnouncementBanner, IndustryTicker, QuickAccessSidebar, ModuleNavBar and SwipeModuleNavigation from layout.tsx:297-304, add the missing carousel exclusions at useModuleNavigation.ts:57, and add one useReducedMotion() hook wired into AnimatedCounter and ScrollReveal (182 call sites fixed by editing one file).

scores.strengths: Cheapest end state in the set and mostly deletion. Its target dark ground means zero ground-migration work. DataTable is the correct diagnosis of the actual gap: 149 files hand-roll <table> and no shared primitive exists, and src/app/rockets/page.tsx really is 82 lines of grid-cols-3 cards over six genuine numeric fields. Wrapping VirtualList and MobileTableView inside it is real reuse. The consolidation targets are precisely right: six freshness/confidence/as-of components -> one StatusBadge; three skeletons -> one RowSkeleton sized to the final row. EmptyState gaining a required reason prop is good API-level enforcement. Reduced motion handled once in globals.css. Its 'would not cut' list is three items that are bugs, not preferences - the Jobs nav mispoint at Navigation.tsx:461, the two 'use client' flagship pages, and the overlay cull. And it grepped mount/persistence logic before filing the offline banner and onboarding modal, exactly the lesson the roadmap asked for.
scores.weaknesses: Its Phase 1 premise is factually wrong for this codebase: 'new token values under existing token names, so every consumer inherits', budgeted at 1.0 day. Only 58 of 1,497 files read var(--text-*). Ship that day of work and the site looks unchanged. Its 'deleted on sight' list includes ScrollReveal, which has 182 call sites - an unpriced 182-file edit hiding inside a line that reads like housekeeping. The DM Sans -> IBM Plex Sans swap is pure risk for no functional gain. 13px base, 3px radius and monochrome ink is the biggest tension with the founder's enthusiast-first priority. And its mockup has a grid defect: at 1440 the MANIFEST and THE WIRE columns end ~150px short of MARKETS.
scores.graft: The DataTable primitive plus the StatusBadge consolidation. One sortable, sticky-header, tabular-nums table that wraps VirtualList past 100 rows and MobileTableView under 640px, plus one <StatusBadge kind asOf>, is the only genuinely reusable new engineering any of the three briefs proposes.

scores.strengths: The only brief that measured the migration cost of its own central idea and then refused to pay it - 929 text-white / 903 bg-white/ / 765 text-slate-400 versus 58 token readers, which I reproduced exactly. It concludes a site-wide ground flip is a 900-file rewrite and moves route by route; Phase 1 ships warm ink (#12100E) so every hardcoded file keeps working untouched. The LiveRail is the single best cost/value item anywhere in these three documents: one cached Prisma call in the root layout replaces LandingHero.tsx:78-133, whose '-' placeholders mean the site's own headline renders as four em-dashes to every crawler. About one day. It also spots that src/lib/charts/* already server-renders SVG + PNG + table + permalink and the front page never links to it. And it is the only brief with a stated kill switch.
scores.weaknesses: Phase 2 is the rewrite this lens exists to penalize. Remapping .text-white, .text-slate-300/400, .bg-white/[0.03] and .border-white/[0.08] under [data-ground="paper"] is a specificity war against Tailwind utilities across 900+ files, and every <svg fill="white">, inline style and one-off inset is an escape hatch the override can't reach. Two grounds doubles the QA surface of every component forever. Fraunces as body copy on the top-traffic SEO pages is a hypothesis to A/B, not a system to build. Phase 1 deletes LandingHero.tsx and rewrites Navigation.tsx from 989 to ~350 lines in the same week - the two most cross-cutting files in the repo. Highest total (22 days), and it nominates its own most distinctive element as cut #1.
scores.graft: The server-rendered LiveRail - one cached Prisma query in layout.tsx rendering a live next-launch line in the HTML on all 129 surfaces, with a static 'Next launch ->' fallback and never a '-'. About a day, design-agnostic. Take the deck component with it.
